questions.q: Which of these lists contains only materials, and no objects?
questions.a: clay, glass, cloth, copper

questions.q: At a chemist shop in Patna, all the syrup bottles are kept on one rack, all the tablet strips on a second rack and all the ointment tubes on a third rack. What is the chemist doing?
questions.a: Classifying the medicines into groups that share a common property
o: Classifying the medicines into groups that share a common property
Choosing the material of each medicine by its purpose
Measuring the mass and volume of each medicine
Testing which medicines are soluble in water

questions.q: Ravi has six objects: a glass marble, a steel ball bearing, a rubber ball, a wooden cube, a steel box and a glass cube. He puts the marble, the ball bearing and the rubber ball in one group, and the other three objects in a second group. Which property has he used to group them?
questions.a: Shape

questions.q:
Match each way of grouping (Column I) with the property used for it (Column II).
Column I: I. Red, blue and green beads are put in three separate boxes.  II. Steel spoons, steel plates and steel tumblers go on one shelf, and wooden ones on another.  III. Marbles, oranges and footballs go in one basket, and books and bricks in another.  IV. Stones go in one pile, and sponges and erasers in another.
Column II: A. Material  B. Colour  C. Hardness  D. Shape
questions.a: I-B, II-A, III-D, IV-C

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A pen can be made of plastic, metal and ink.
Reason (R): Different materials may be used for making different parts of one object.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) What is meant by a material?
(b) An umbrella has a cloth cover, metal rods and a plastic handle. Is it made of a single material or of a combination of materials? Name them.
questions.a: (a) Any substance that is used to create an object is called a material. (b) It is made of a combination of materials: cloth, metal and plastic.
s: (a) Defines a material as any substance used to create an object
(b) Says it is a combination of materials and names cloth, metal and plastic

questions.q: True or False? A plastic bucket and a plastic comb are made of the same material, so they must be used for the same purpose. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. One material can be used to make more than one object. Plastic is used to make a bucket, which holds water, and also a comb, which is used for hair; their uses are quite different.
s: States the verdict: False
Explains that one material can make several objects with different uses, e.g. the bucket and the comb

questions.q:
(a) What is classification?
(b) Name any two properties on which objects can be grouped.
(c) Name one place, at home or in a shop, where things are kept in such groups.
questions.a: (a) The method of arranging objects into groups on the basis of a common property is called classification. (b) Any two of: shape, colour, hardness or softness, shine or dullness, the material the objects are made of. (c) For example, a kitchen where similar utensils are kept together, a grocer's shop with spices in one corner and pulses and grains in another, or a chemist shop.
s: (a) Defines classification as arranging objects into groups by a common property
(b) Names two valid properties such as shape, colour, hardness, shine or material
(c) Names a place where things are grouped, such as a kitchen, a grocer's or a chemist shop

questions.q:
Ritu says: 'Tumblers are made of steel, glass, plastic and clay, so any material at all can be used to make a tumbler.'
(a) Which part of her statement is correct?
(b) Which part is wrong? Give an example of a material that would not work.
(c) State the rule for choosing a material for an object.
questions.a: (a) Correct: the same object can be made from different materials, as tumblers are made of steel, glass, plastic or clay. (b) Wrong: not every material works. A tumbler must be able to hold water, so a tumbler made of cloth cannot be used to store water. (c) A material is chosen depending on its properties and the purpose for which the object is to be used.
s: (a) Agrees that one object can be made from several different materials
(b) Rejects 'any material' with a valid example such as cloth, which cannot hold water
(c) States that a material is chosen by its properties and the purpose of the object

questions.q:
The lost-and-found box of a school in Indore holds 6 steel water bottles, 3 plastic water bottles, 4 plastic lunch boxes, 2 steel lunch boxes, 5 woollen caps and 2 cotton caps. The caretaker wants to arrange these 22 items on shelves, one group to a shelf, so that children can find what they have lost.
(a) If he groups the items by the material they are made of, how many groups does he get, and which group is the largest?
(b) If he groups them instead by the kind of object (bottle, lunch box or cap), how many items are in the largest group?
(c) In which of the two groupings does a steel bottle sit on the same shelf as a steel lunch box?
(d) Children come asking for 'my bottle' or 'my cap'. Which grouping should the caretaker use for them? Justify using your answers to (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Four groups: steel 6 + 2 = 8, plastic 3 + 4 = 7, wool 5 and cotton 2; the steel group (8 items) is the largest. (b) Bottles: 6 + 3 = 9 items (caps 7, lunch boxes 6), so the largest group has 9 items. (c) In the grouping by material. (d) By kind of object: then all 9 bottles are on one shelf and all 7 caps on another. In the grouping by material, a child's bottle could be on the steel shelf or the plastic shelf, and a cap on the wool shelf or the cotton shelf, so she would have to search two shelves. Both are correct classifications; the purpose decides which one to use.
s: (a) Finds 4 groups by material and names steel (8 items) as the largest
(b) Finds 9 bottles as the largest group by kind of object
(c) Names the grouping by material
(d) Chooses grouping by kind of object and explains that the material grouping splits bottles and caps over two shelves each

questions.q:
A school in Hubballi is making a reading corner. The class has tested five materials and found these properties.
Glass sheet: hard, transparent.
Plywood: hard, opaque.
Cotton cloth: soft, opaque, can be folded.
Butter paper: soft, translucent, tears easily.
Foam: soft, opaque, compressed easily.
Using only this list, choose a material for each part and give the property that decides it.
(a) A window between the corridor and the reading corner, through which the teacher can see the children clearly.
(b) The filling of floor cushions, which should be compressed easily when children sit on them.
(c) A shelf back that must be hard and must hide the cleaning things kept behind it.
(d) A curtain that can be pulled across and folded away.
(e) A student suggests butter paper for the window in (a) because 'light comes through it'. Is this a good choice? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Glass sheet: it is the only transparent material, so things can be seen clearly through it. (b) Foam: it is the only material that is compressed easily. (c) Plywood: it is hard and opaque (glass is hard but transparent, so it would not hide anything). (d) Cotton cloth: it is the only material that can be folded. (e) No. Butter paper is translucent, so the teacher would see the children but not clearly; it also tears easily. A material is chosen by its properties and the purpose of the object.
s: (a) Chooses the glass sheet because it is transparent
(b) Chooses foam because it is compressed easily
(c) Chooses plywood because it is hard and opaque
(d) Chooses cotton cloth because it can be folded
(e) Rejects butter paper because it is translucent (not clear) and tears easily

questions.q: Which of these has a lustrous appearance?
questions.a: A new copper wire

questions.q: A shop in Moradabad has two copper plates cut from the same sheet. One was kept in a dry glass cabinet and still shines. The other was kept near a damp, open window for a year and now looks dull. Which statement best explains the difference?
questions.a: Air and moisture have dulled the surface of the plate near the window
o: Air and moisture have dulled the surface of the plate near the window
The plate near the window has changed into a non-metal
Copper shows lustre only when it is kept behind glass
The plate near the window has become softer than the other

questions.q:
Read these statements.
I. Paper, wood and jute are non-lustrous materials.
II. Every material that shines is a metal.
III. Iron, copper and zinc are examples of metals.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q:
A craft teacher in Jaipur cuts a tiny fresh spot on the base of four pieces.
P: shiny outside; the fresh spot is shiny.
Q: dull outside; the fresh spot is shiny.
R: shiny outside; the fresh spot is dull and brown, like wood.
S: dull outside; the fresh spot is dull.
Which pieces are most likely made of metal?
questions.a: P and Q only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A wooden table polished with wax can look shiny.
Reason (R): The surfaces of some materials are made shiny by polishing or by coating them with thin layers of wax, plastic or other materials.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Seeing that an object shines is not enough to prove that it is made of metal.
Reason (R): Some metals lose their lustre due to the effect of air and moisture on them.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) What are lustrous materials?
(b) Name two non-lustrous materials.
questions.a: (a) Materials that have a shiny surface are said to be lustrous; they are usually metals. (b) Any two of: paper, wood, rubber, jute.
s: (a) Says lustrous materials have a shiny surface
(b) Names two non-lustrous materials such as paper, wood, rubber or jute

questions.q: True or False? An old, dull iron nail and a new, shiny iron nail are made of the same kind of material, even though they look different. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Both nails are made of iron, a metal. The old nail has lost its lustre because of the effect of air and moisture on it; a freshly cut surface of it would still show lustre.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that both are iron and the old one lost its lustre due to air and moisture

questions.q:
Look at these six objects: a new gold chain, a jute bag, a fresh piece of aluminium foil, a wooden spoon, a new copper wire and a rubber slipper.
(a) List the lustrous objects.
(b) List the non-lustrous objects.
(c) The lustrous materials here are usually of which kind?
questions.a: (a) The gold chain, the aluminium foil and the copper wire. (b) The jute bag, the wooden spoon and the rubber slipper. (c) They are metals (gold, aluminium and copper).
s: (a) Lists the gold chain, aluminium foil and copper wire as lustrous
(b) Lists the jute bag, wooden spoon and rubber slipper as non-lustrous
(c) Says lustrous materials are usually metals

questions.q:
A small museum in Hyderabad is moving objects into a new 'Metal Crafts' room. A worker checks each object by looking at its outer surface and at a tiny freshly cut spot on its base.
Object W: outer surface dark and dull; cut spot shiny.
Object X: outer surface bright and shiny; cut spot dull and brown, like wood.
Object Y: outer surface bright and shiny; cut spot shiny.
Object Z: outer surface dull and brown; cut spot dull.
(a) Which objects should go into the Metal Crafts room?
(b) Why does W look dull although it belongs there?
(c) Why can X shine although it does not belong there?
(d) The guide wants to sort by the outer surface alone. Name the two objects that this rule would put in the wrong room.
(e) Write a two-step rule the worker can use to check any new object.
questions.a: (a) W and Y, because their freshly cut spots show lustre, so they are most likely metals. (b) W is a metal whose surface has lost its lustre due to the effect of air and moisture; the fresh cut shows the lustre underneath. (c) X is probably wood whose surface has been made shiny by polishing or by a thin coating of wax, plastic or another material; the cut spot shows it is non-lustrous inside. (d) W (dull, so it would be left out although it is a metal) and X (shiny, so it would be put in although it is not a metal). (e) Step 1: look at a freshly cut or scraped spot, not the old outer surface. Step 2: if the fresh spot shines, treat the object as a metal; if it is dull, it is not a metal, however the outside looks.
s: (a) Chooses W and Y using the shiny cut spots
(b) Explains that W lost its lustre due to air and moisture
(c) Explains that X was made shiny by polishing or coating and is not a metal
(d) Names W and X as the two objects the outer-surface rule gets wrong
(e) Gives a rule based on checking a freshly cut surface for lustre

questions.q: Tara scratches a candle, a stick of chalk and an iron nail with the same metal key, pressing equally each time. The candle gets a deep scratch, the chalk gets a light scratch and the iron nail gets no scratch. Which list goes from the hardest to the softest?
questions.a: iron nail, chalk, candle

questions.q:
Read these statements.
I. A material that is hard when compared with a sponge may be soft when compared with iron.
II. A stone is called hard because it is difficult to compress or scratch.
III. A material that has once been called hard is harder than every other material.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A stone is called a hard material.
Reason (R): A stone can be compressed easily with the hands.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Differentiate between hard and soft materials. Give one example of each.
questions.a: Hard materials are difficult to compress or scratch, for example stone or iron. Soft materials can be compressed or scratched easily, for example an eraser or a sponge.
s: Says hard materials are difficult to compress or scratch, with an example such as stone or iron
Says soft materials are compressed or scratched easily, with an example such as an eraser or sponge

questions.q: True or False? If a metal key cannot scratch a material, then nothing at all can scratch that material. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Hardness is relative. The key test only shows that the material is not softer than the key; a material harder than it could still scratch it.
s: States the verdict: False
Explains that hardness is relative, so the key test only compares the material with the key

questions.q:
Say whether each object is hard or soft, and name the main material it is made of.
(a) A woollen sweater
(b) A wooden table
(c) A cotton-filled pillow
questions.a: (a) Soft; wool. (b) Hard; wood. (c) Soft; cotton.
s: (a) Soft, made of wool
(b) Hard, made of wood
(c) Soft, filled with cotton

questions.q:
A toy-maker in Channapatna tests four materials. He presses each one with his thumb and scratches each one with the same metal key.
Wet clay: compressed a lot; scratched very easily.
Cork: compressed a little; scratched easily.
Seasoned wood: not compressed; scratched only with effort.
Iron: not compressed; not scratched.
(a) Arrange the four materials from the softest to the hardest.
(b) Which material is hard when compared with cork, but soft when compared with iron?
(c) He needs a material for the axle of a toy cart, which must not be compressed or scratched in use. Which should he choose?
(d) His helper says, 'Cork is a soft material.' Use the data to explain whether this is fully correct.
questions.a: (a) Wet clay, cork, seasoned wood, iron. (b) Seasoned wood: it is not compressed and is harder to scratch than cork, but the key scratches it while it cannot scratch iron. (c) Iron, because it was neither compressed nor scratched. (d) Only partly correct: cork is soft compared with wood and iron, but it is harder than wet clay, which is compressed more and scratched more easily. Hardness and softness are relative, so 'soft' needs the comparison.
s: (a) Orders wet clay, cork, seasoned wood, iron
(b) Names seasoned wood with evidence from both tests
(c) Chooses iron because it was neither compressed nor scratched
(d) Explains that cork is soft compared with wood and iron but harder than wet clay, so hardness is relative

questions.q:
Class 6 students in Mysuru test five classroom objects. They press each object with a hand and try to scratch it with a metal key.
Chalk stick: not compressed; scratched easily.
Rubber eraser: compressed easily; scratched easily.
Wooden ruler: not compressed; scratched only with effort.
Steel scale: not compressed; not scratched.
Foam duster: compressed very easily; scratched very easily.
(a) Which two objects could be compressed easily?
(b) Which object could not be scratched by the key?
(c) Is the wooden ruler harder or softer than the rubber eraser? Give the evidence.
(d) Arrange the foam duster, the wooden ruler and the steel scale from the softest to the hardest.
questions.a: (a) The rubber eraser and the foam duster. (b) The steel scale. (c) Harder: the ruler was not compressed and was scratched only with effort, while the eraser was compressed and scratched easily. (d) Foam duster, wooden ruler, steel scale.
s: (a) Names the rubber eraser and the foam duster
(b) Names the steel scale
(c) Says the ruler is harder, using the compress and scratch results
(d) Orders foam duster, wooden ruler, steel scale

questions.q:
Engineers in Kota are building a playground. They press each material by hand and try to scratch it with a metal key.
Foam sheet: compressed a lot; scratched very easily.
Rubber mat: compressed a little; scratched easily.
Wooden plank: not compressed; scratched only with effort.
Concrete slab: not compressed; not scratched.
Iron pipe: not compressed; not scratched.
(a) Arrange the foam sheet, the rubber mat and the wooden plank from the softest to the hardest.
(b) Explain why the rubber mat can be called both hard and soft.
(c) The ground under the swings must be softer than the wooden plank but harder than the foam sheet. Which material fits?
(d) Can the concrete slab and the iron pipe be put in order of hardness using only these two tests? Explain.
(e) Suggest one test that would settle which of the two is harder, and say how to read the result.
questions.a: (a) Foam sheet, rubber mat, wooden plank. (b) Hardness is relative: the rubber mat is harder than the foam sheet (it is compressed less and scratched less easily) but softer than the wooden plank (it is compressed and scratched more easily). (c) The rubber mat. (d) No. Both were neither compressed by hand nor scratched by the key, so these tests give the same result for both and cannot rank them. (e) Try to scratch one with the other: the material that scratches the other is the harder one.
s: (a) Orders foam sheet, rubber mat, wooden plank
(b) Explains that the rubber mat is harder than foam but softer than wood, so hardness is relative
(c) Chooses the rubber mat
(d) Says the two cannot be ranked because both gave the same results in both tests
(e) Suggests scratching one with the other; the one that scratches is harder

questions.q: Through which of these can objects be seen, but not clearly?
questions.a: Butter paper

questions.q: At a railway station in Bhopal, Neha stands behind a large cardboard advertisement board. Her friend on the other side cannot see her at all. What kind of material is the board made of?
questions.a: Opaque

questions.q:
Match each word (Column I) with a material from the chapter that it describes (Column II).
Column I: I. Transparent  II. Translucent  III. Opaque  IV. Soluble in water
Column II: A. Cellophane paper  B. Frosted glass  C. Wooden board  D. Salt
questions.a: I-A, II-B, III-C, IV-D

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Butter paper is a translucent material.
Reason (R): Through a translucent material, objects can be seen clearly.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) What are opaque materials?
(b) Name two opaque materials.
questions.a: (a) Materials through which we are not able to see at all are called opaque. (b) Any two of: wood, cardboard, metals (for example an iron sheet).
s: (a) Says opaque materials are those through which we cannot see at all
(b) Names two opaque materials such as wood, cardboard or a metal

questions.q: True or False? If you can make out the shape of an object through a sheet, the sheet must be transparent. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Through a translucent sheet, such as butter paper or frosted glass, objects can be seen but not clearly. A sheet is transparent only if things can be seen clearly through it.
s: States the verdict: False
Explains that translucent materials also let objects be seen, but not clearly, with an example

questions.q:
In a bank in Nagpur, a customer stands in front of three places. For each, say whether she can see a person behind it clearly, not clearly, or not at all, and name the type of material.
(a) The cashier's counter, behind a clear glass screen.
(b) The manager's cabin, behind a frosted glass door.
(c) The locker room, behind an iron door.
questions.a: (a) Clearly; clear glass is transparent. (b) Not clearly; frosted glass is translucent. (c) Not at all; iron, a metal, is opaque.
s: (a) Clearly; transparent
(b) Not clearly; translucent
(c) Not at all; opaque

questions.q:
Mira has three sheets of the same size: cellophane paper, butter paper and cardboard.
(a) Which sheet should cover a tray of seeds so that she can watch them clearly every day? Give the property.
(b) Which sheet should she use as a shade for a night lamp, so that the light glows softly but the bulb is not seen clearly? Give the property.
(c) Her brother says a gift can be wrapped in butter paper to hide it, 'because butter paper is not transparent'. Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Cellophane paper, because it is transparent: things can be seen clearly through it. (b) Butter paper, because it is translucent: light comes through but the bulb is not seen clearly. (c) No. Butter paper is not transparent, but it is translucent, not opaque, so the shape of the gift could still be made out. To hide the gift she needs an opaque sheet such as cardboard.
s: (a) Chooses cellophane paper because it is transparent
(b) Chooses butter paper because it is translucent
(c) Rejects the claim: butter paper is translucent, not opaque, so an opaque sheet such as cardboard is needed

questions.q:
A Class 6 group in Ranchi holds five sheets, one at a time, between their eyes and a lit candle placed 1 m away, and records what they see.
Glass sheet: the flame and the wick are seen clearly.
Butter paper: only a blurred glow is seen.
Wooden plank: nothing is seen.
Frosted glass: only a blurred glow is seen.
Aluminium foil: nothing is seen.
(a) Which sheets are opaque?
(b) Which sheets are translucent?
(c) The aluminium foil and the wooden plank fall in the same group in this test. Would they stay together if the sheets were sorted by lustre? Explain.
(d) The staff room needs a window in its door that lets light in but keeps the room private, and that will last for years on a door opened and shut all day. Which sheet should be chosen? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The wooden plank and the aluminium foil. (b) The butter paper and the frosted glass. (c) No. Aluminium foil is a metal with a shiny (lustrous) surface, while wood is non-lustrous, so sorting by lustre would split them, though both are opaque. (d) Frosted glass: it is translucent, so light comes in but people inside are not seen clearly. Butter paper is also translucent, but it is a soft paper that would not last on a door; the glass sheet is transparent and would not keep the room private.
s: (a) Names the wooden plank and the aluminium foil as opaque
(b) Names the butter paper and the frosted glass as translucent
(c) Says they would be split because aluminium foil is lustrous and wood is non-lustrous
(d) Chooses frosted glass as translucent and rejects the glass sheet (transparent) and butter paper (would not last)

questions.q: A sari shop wants a cabinet door through which customers can see the colours and designs of the saris clearly. Ravi suggests frosted glass 'because it is glass and lets light in'. What is wrong with his choice?
questions.a: Frosted glass is translucent, so the saris would be seen but not clearly
o: Frosted glass is translucent, so the saris would be seen but not clearly
Frosted glass is opaque, so the saris could not be seen at all
Frosted glass is lustrous, so its shine would hide the saris
Frosted glass is transparent, so it would show too much of the shop

questions.q:
Four sheets of the same size, P, Q, R and S, are held one at a time 30 cm in front of a printed eye-test chart under a bright light.
P: even the smallest line of letters can be read.
Q: only the dark outline of the chart can be made out; no letter can be read.
R: nothing of the chart can be seen.
S: the smallest letters can be read; after one side of S is rubbed with sandpaper until it looks hazy, only the outline of the chart can be made out.
(a) Classify P, Q and R as transparent, translucent or opaque.
(b) Classify S before rubbing and after rubbing.
(c) What does S show about whether a material's see-through nature depends only on what it is made of?
(d) A doctor wants a window in her clinic door that lets light in but does not let patients inside be seen clearly. Which sheet, as tested, suits her? Give a reason.
(e) P is placed on top of R and held in front of the chart. Can the chart be seen? Explain.
questions.a: (a) P is transparent, Q is translucent and R is opaque. (b) S is transparent before rubbing and translucent after rubbing. (c) It does not depend only on the material: the same sheet became translucent when its surface was made hazy, just as frosted glass, which has a hazy surface, is translucent while plain glass is transparent. (d) Q (or S after rubbing): it is translucent, so light passes but people behind it are not seen clearly. (e) No. R is opaque, so nothing can be seen through it, whatever transparent sheet is placed with it.
s: (a) Classifies P transparent, Q translucent, R opaque
(b) Classifies S as transparent before and translucent after rubbing
(c) Explains that a hazy surface can make a see-through material translucent, as with frosted glass
(d) Chooses Q (or rubbed S) because it is translucent
(e) Says the chart cannot be seen because R is opaque

questions.q: Farah stirs a spoonful of a white powder into a glass of water. After waiting a few minutes, she can still see the powder lying at the bottom. What can she say about this powder?
questions.a: It is insoluble in water

questions.q:
Read these statements.
I. Every liquid forms a separate layer when it is mixed with water.
II. Oxygen gas dissolves in water.
III. Sugar is soluble in water, but sawdust is insoluble.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Some liquids form a separate layer when they are mixed with water and left undisturbed.
Reason (R): Water can dissolve a large number of materials.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Animals that live in water can get oxygen from the water around them.
Reason (R): Oxygen gas dissolves in water.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) A spoonful of salt is stirred into a jug of water and can no longer be seen. Is salt soluble or insoluble in water?
(b) Name one material from the chapter that would still be seen after it is stirred in water.
questions.a: (a) Soluble, because it disappeared completely on stirring. (b) Sand (or sawdust).
s: (a) Says salt is soluble because it disappeared on stirring
(b) Names an insoluble material such as sand or sawdust

questions.q: True or False? A spoon of sugar and a spoon of sand are stirred together into a glass of water. After a few minutes, only the sand can still be seen. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Sugar is soluble in water, so it disappears on stirring; sand is insoluble, so it does not disappear and can still be seen.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that sugar is soluble and disappears while sand is insoluble and stays visible

questions.q:
At a science fair, each of four jars of water has had one material stirred into it, and the jars have then been left undisturbed for 10 minutes.
Jar 1: the water is clear and nothing else is seen.
Jar 2: solid bits are floating on top.
Jar 3: a solid is lying at the bottom.
Jar 4: a layer of another liquid is floating on the water.
(a) Which jar most likely holds a material that is soluble in water?
(b) Which jars show a material that is insoluble in water or does not mix with it?
(c) What does Jar 4 tell you about liquids and water?
questions.a: (a) Jar 1, because the material has disappeared completely. (b) Jars 2, 3 and 4: their materials can still be seen after stirring and waiting. (c) Some liquids do not mix with water and form a separate layer when left undisturbed.
s: (a) Names Jar 1, because the material disappeared
(b) Names Jars 2, 3 and 4, because the material is still seen
(c) States that some liquids do not mix with water and form a separate layer

questions.q:
A dhaba in Amritsar makes 30 glasses of shikanji every evening. To save time, a new helper puts all the sugar for the evening into one large jug of water and stirs; after stirring, the water is clear. The next day, by mistake, he uses a jar of fine sand that looks just like sugar. He stirs well, but after 10 minutes the sand can still be seen at the bottom of the jug.
(a) Why did the sugar water look clear after stirring?
(b) What observation showed that the second jar did not hold sugar?
(c) The helper says, 'If I stir for longer, the sand will also disappear.' Is he right? Give a reason.
(d) The owner wants every unlabelled white powder checked before use. Should the helper check it by looking at it, or by stirring a pinch into a glass of water and waiting? Justify your choice, and name one thing this water test cannot tell him.
questions.a: (a) Sugar is soluble in water: it disappears completely when stirred. (b) The material did not disappear; it was still seen at the bottom after stirring and waiting, so it was insoluble, unlike sugar. (c) No. Insoluble materials such as sand do not disappear even after they are stirred for a long time. (d) Stirring a pinch into water: sugar and fine sand can look alike, but a soluble material disappears and an insoluble one stays visible. The test cannot tell apart two soluble powders, such as sugar and salt, because both disappear in water.
s: (a) Explains that sugar is soluble and disappears on stirring
(b) Uses the sand still being visible after stirring and waiting as the evidence
(c) Says no: insoluble materials do not disappear even after long stirring
(d) Chooses the water test with a reason and notes it cannot separate two soluble powders such as sugar and salt

questions.q:
After a class activity on mixing materials in water, a group writes five conclusions. Say whether each one is correct, and correct the wrong ones.
(i) 'Sugar is soluble in water, because it disappeared completely when we stirred it.'
(ii) 'Sand is soluble in water, because the water turned cloudy for a moment while we were stirring it.'
(iii) 'Sawdust is insoluble in water, because it could still be seen after stirring and waiting.'
(iv) 'No gas can dissolve in water, because we cannot see any gas in a glass of water.'
(v) 'Because oil formed a separate layer, no liquid can mix completely with water.'
questions.a: (i) Correct: a material that disappears completely on stirring is soluble. (ii) Wrong: sand is insoluble; it does not disappear even after long stirring and is seen again once the water is left to stand. (iii) Correct: a material that is still seen after stirring is insoluble. (iv) Wrong: some gases are soluble in water; oxygen dissolves in water and is very important for the animals and plants that live in water. (v) Wrong: some liquids do not mix and form a separate layer, but other liquids get completely mixed with water.
s: (i) Marks it correct with the reason that sugar disappears completely
(ii) Marks it wrong: sand is insoluble and does not disappear even after long stirring
(iii) Marks it correct with the reason that sawdust is still seen
(iv) Marks it wrong, giving oxygen as a gas that dissolves in water
(v) Marks it wrong: some liquids mix completely with water while others form a layer

questions.q: How should three hundred and fifty millilitres be written using the unit symbol?
questions.a: 350 mL

questions.q: A village water tank holds 3 m³ of water. Given that 1 m³ = 1000 L, how much water does it hold in litres?

Match each quantity (Column I) with the unit best suited to measure it (Column II).
Column I: I. The mass of a watermelon  II. The volume of juice in a small glass  III. The volume of water in a large underground tank  IV. The mass of a pencil
Column II: A. kilogram (kg)  B. millilitre (mL)  C. cubic metre (m³)  D. gram (g)
questions.a: I-A, II-B, III-C, IV-D

questions.q:
Read these statements.
I. Air has mass and occupies space, so air is matter.
II. The water in a cup is matter, but the cup itself is not.
III. A mass of 7 kilograms is correctly written as 7 kgs.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A tank holding 1 m³ of water holds less than 100 L of water.
Reason (R): 1 m³ = 1000 L.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
(a) What is volume?
(b) Write the correct unit symbols for litre and for millilitre.
questions.a: (a) The space occupied by matter (a material) is its volume. (b) Litre: L (capital L). Millilitre: mL (small m and capital L, with no space between them).
s: (a) Defines volume as the space occupied by matter
(b) Writes L for litre and mL for millilitre

questions.q:
Each quantity below is written wrongly. Rewrite each one correctly and state the rule it breaks.
(a) 9 k g
(b) 250 m L
(c) 3L
questions.a: (a) 9 kg: there is no space between 'k' and 'g'. (b) 250 mL: there is no space between 'm' and 'L'. (c) 3 L: always leave a space between the number and the unit.
s: (a) Writes 9 kg and states there is no space between k and g
(b) Writes 250 mL and states there is no space between m and L
(c) Writes 3 L and states a space is left between the number and the unit

questions.q:
A school stores water in drums that hold 200 L each. Use 1 m³ = 1000 L and 1 L = 1000 mL.
(a) How many full drums hold 1 m³ of water?
(b) How many full drums are needed for 2 m³ of water?
(c) How many bottles of 500 mL can be filled from one full drum?
s: (a) Converts 1 m³ to 1000 L and finds 5 drums
(b) Finds 10 drums for 2000 L
(c) Converts 200 L to 2,00,000 mL and finds 400 bottles

questions.q:
A shop in Shillong receives a 6 kg sack of jaggery. The shopkeeper packs it into packets of 500 g and 250 g. Use 1 kg = 1000 g.
(a) Write the mass of the sack in grams.
(b) How many 250 g packets could he fill if he used only 250 g packets?
(c) He first fills 8 packets of 500 g. How many 250 g packets can he fill with the jaggery that is left?
(d) His labels read '500 gms' and '250 G'. Rewrite both labels correctly and state the rule each one breaks.
questions.a: (a) 6 kg = 6 x 1000 = 6000 g. (b) 6000 / 250 = 24 packets. (c) 8 x 500 = 4000 g used; 6000 - 4000 = 2000 g left; 2000 / 250 = 8 packets. (d) '500 g': a unit symbol takes no plural 's'. '250 g': the symbol for gram is written in lower case.
s: (a) Converts 6 kg to 6000 g
(b) Finds 24 packets of 250 g
(c) Finds 2000 g left and 8 packets of 250 g
(d) Rewrites both labels as 500 g and 250 g, naming the no-plural and lower-case rules

questions.q:
A school in Ajmer is buying drinking water for its sports day. Each of its 600 students needs 500 mL. The water can be bought in 20 L cans at Rs 70 each (poured into cups at the ground) or in 1 L bottles at Rs 20 each. Use 1 L = 1000 mL.
(a) Find the total volume of water needed in millilitres.
(b) Write this volume in litres.
(c) How many 20 L cans are needed, and what will they cost?
(d) What will the 1 L bottles cost? The principal prefers the cans and the sports teacher prefers the bottles. Decide which to buy, giving one point from the figures and one point on the other side.
(e) The clerk writes the total on the order form as '300 l'. Rewrite it correctly and give the rule.
questions.a: (a) 600 x 500 = 3,00,000 mL. (b) 3,00,000 / 1000 = 300 L. (c) 300 / 20 = 15 cans, costing 15 x 70 = Rs 1,050. (d) 300 bottles cost 300 x 20 = Rs 6,000. Cans save Rs 6,000 - Rs 1,050 = Rs 4,950, so buy the cans; on the other side, bottles need no cups and each child can carry her own water. (A reasoned choice of bottles that uses the figures also earns the mark.) (e) 300 L: the litre is written with a capital L, with a space between the number and the unit.
s: (a) Finds 3,00,000 mL
(b) Converts to 300 L
(c) Finds 15 cans costing Rs 1,050
(d) Finds Rs 6,000 for bottles and makes a decision using the Rs 4,950 difference and one point on the other side
(e) Writes 300 L with a capital L and a space
